report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Misinformation and conspiracy theories are often treated as interchangeable, but they have different predictors and respond differently to correction.
We identify their differences at the level of the claim itself rather than at what these claims trigger in the mind of the believer.
Whereas misinformation claims are, in principle, assessable against a ground truth, conspiracy theories are claims wrapped in an explanation for why evidence is absent or untrustworthy.
This semantic criterion avoids conflating bare falsehoods with conspiracy theories while preserving the distinctive structural features of the latter.
We show how the wrapper grants conspiracy theories a degree of immunity from disconfirmation and why a claim-level demarcation can inform both theory and measurement.

In July 2026, ahead of the US midterm elections, President Donald J. Trump (once again, Jacobson, 2023; Lewandowsky, Lloyd, & Brophy, 2018) raised concerns about electoral integrity, claiming that FBI files revealed "evidence of alleged fraud by a large-scale voter registration operation in Michigan", and that "even when significant evidence of fraud has been detected, it has been buried and covered up". 1Most readers would label these two assertions as misinformation, conspiracy theories, or both.

Trump (once again, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Jacobson, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lewandowsky, Lloyd, & Brophy, 2018)</ref> raised concerns about electoral integrity, claiming that FBI files revealed "evidence of alleged fraud by a large-scale voter registration operation in Michigan", and that "even when significant evidence of fraud has been detected, it has been buried and covered up". <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref>Most readers would label these two assertions as misinformation, conspiracy theories, or both.

text.text: But which are they?
And if officials were involved in the concealment, could evidence ever confirm or reject them?
These questions expose two related problems in research on misinformation and conspiracy theories (CTs), whose definitions are fuzzy, and so are their boundaries (Scantamburlo & Zollo, 2026).

text.text: For example, in a systematic review of 148 studies on CTs published between 2007 and 2020, Mahl et al. (2022) found that 72.3% referred to misinformation and CTs interchangeably without explicitly defining or differentiating them, and that nearly half (43.9%) invoked several terms simultaneously without delineation.

(2022)</ref> found that 72.3% referred to misinformation and CTs interchangeably without explicitly defining or differentiating them, and that nearly half (43.9%) invoked several terms simultaneously without delineation.

text.text: Without a settled definition and criteria for demarcation, operationalizations will inevitably vary, and so will their measurement and estimated prevalence.
In this chapter we attempt to resolve both problems, at least in part, by demarcating misinformation and CTs at the level of claims.
Our demarcation rests on a single criterion: a claim's relationship to truth, as determined by its structure and content, deliberately setting aside the beliefs and motives of those who endorse them.

We suspect that much of the definitional confusion has arisen because the pragmatic interpretation of claims (what a claim suggests to its audience in context, as opposed to what it actually states) has been absorbed into the definitions themselves.
Our demarcation therefore deliberately shifts from a pragmatic to a semantic reading: we classify claims by what they assert, not by what they may lead an audience to infer.
Consider the claims made by President Trump.
Taken pragmatically, both imply a conspiracy: that a large-scale, organized operation fraudulently registered voters in Michigan, and that government officials deliberately buried the evidence.
Yet the two are structurally different.

The first is a factual, checkable claim about the scale and nature of the fraud: taken on its own, it is falsifiable and correctable. 2 The second adds an account of why the first cannot be checked: because a successful concealment leaves no detectable trace, the assertion now explains the very absence of evidence that would otherwise count against it.

text.text: CTs are thus distinguished from misinformation by this additional content, which, wrapped around a factual claim, makes the overall assertion resistant to disconfirmation: neither missing nor contrary evidence can refute it.

In a review of 410 empirical studies on misinformation, Scantamburlo and Zollo (2026) found that 39% offer no conceptual definition at all and 10% lack both a conceptual and an operational one; among those that did define the term, definitions varied substantially across disciplines.

text.text: Different definitions shape what gets counted as misinformation.

Stricter vs. broader definitions (e.g., including hyperpartisan content) yield different estimates of the scale of the problem, and have produced two opposed research positions ("minimizing" vs. "alarmist"; see Ecker et al., 2024).

text.text: A recent EU expert report, however, reframes them as a false dichotomy, noting that the most consequential harm stems from accuratebut-misleading content and elite rhetoric, which are harder to verify (Scharfbillig et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent EU expert report, however, reframes them as a false dichotomy, noting that the most consequential harm stems from accuratebut-misleading content and elite rhetoric, which are harder to verify <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Scharfbillig et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As an umbrella term, misinformation generally includes information that is inaccurate, false, accurate but misleading, or unsubstantiated (Ecker et al., 2022; Scantamburlo & Zollo, 2026).
text.formatted: As an umbrella term, misinformation generally includes information that is inaccurate, false, accurate but misleading, or unsubstantiated <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ecker et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Scantamburlo & Zollo, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these cases represents a different way a claim relates to a ground truth that is based on the best available evidence from relevant experts at the time.
The first two cases, inaccuracy and falsity, are precision failures to correspond to truth.
A claim such as "the population of the USA in 2026 is 320 million people" is inaccurate relative to the official 2026 figure of 340 million, without being blatantly false in the categorical sense.
Sufficiently large errors, however, become categorical false claims, such as "the Earth is flat" and "vaccines cause autism".
The third case, misleadingness, refers to claims that are not technically false or imprecise yet still produce a false impression in the audience.

For example, a Chicago Tribune headline reporting that a healthy doctor died two weeks after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine was factually accurate, yet implied a causal link that had not been established (Allen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, a Chicago Tribune headline reporting that a healthy doctor died two weeks after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine was factually accurate, yet implied a causal link that had not been established <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Misleadingness also includes cherry-picking, which consists in selectively citing a factually true claim to support a conclusion that the full evidence would not warrant.

In climate-change denial, for example, the claim that "global tem-peratures fell from 2016 to 2018" is not technically false, yet, stripped of context, it creates a false impression about the long-term trend (Cook, 2020).
text.formatted: In climate-change denial, for example, the claim that "global tem-peratures fell from 2016 to 2018" is not technically false, yet, stripped of context, it creates a false impression about the long-term trend <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cook, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly deceptive are claims so vague that they are uninformative rather than false, such as Barnum statements and pseudo-profound bullshit.

Common in mental-health misinformation (Starvaggi et al., 2024), they mislead by framing universally applicable descriptions as if they were individually diagnostic ("if you sometimes find it hard to say no, it may be a trauma response").

text.text: Unsubstantiation, another form of misinformation, differs from the previous three in that it lies beyond the true/false dichotomy.
An unsubstantiated claim cannot be checked against a ground truth because the relevant evidence has not yet been gathered.
A claim such as "placing a halved onion in a room prevents the flu" is neither false nor true, because no evidence exists.

Unsubstantiated claims vary widely in prior plausibility (compare the onion claim with the claim that there is an onion in one's neighbor's kitchen), but unsubstantiation is not a permanent condition: evidence can in principle be collected (by checking the kitchen, or by testing onions in clinical trials), and once it exists, the claim can be assessed against the truth.
All these claims are truth-apt: whatever their specific relationship with truth, each can be assessed against a ground truth and is therefore falsifiable.

The epistemic gap they create can, in principle, be closed by evidence: a false claim can be replaced with a true one, an inaccurate figure can be updated, a misleading framing can be explained by supplying context, and an unsubstantiated claim can wait for evidence.
In each case, nothing in the claim itself prevents evidence from being gathered and weighed.
This, as we argue below, is the sharpest difference from CTs.
As with misinformation, no shared consensus exists on what CTs actually are, and different operationalizations shape what gets counted as a CT.
The LOCO corpus (Miani et al., 2021), for example, includes webpages on topics popularly associated with CTs, such as Bigfoot and the deaths of Elvis Presley and Princess Diana.

text.text: The problem is that it is not obvious what makes these topics CTs rather than merely unsubstantiated stories (Uscinski, 2025).

text.text: Research into the psychology of CTs faces a similar measurement problem.
Aside from two notable exceptions that separate the two constructs (Piliousis & Gardikiotis, 2026; Zwolinski, 2024), CTs and misinformation are often conflated.

text.text: Yet, as we argue next, the narrative content of CTs gives them properties that make them highly resistant to disconfirmation and capable of explaining any event.

As Keeley (1999) observed, unlike science, which studies an object indifferent to being measured (e.g., nature), CTs describe a domain whose object of inves-tigation actively obstructs the investigation: "Imagine if neutrinos were not simply hard to detect, but actively sought to avoid detection!"

text.text: Because a conspiracy is a covert action whose success depends on remaining undiscovered, a perfectly functioning conspiracy leaves no trace, and the absence of evidence is read as a sign of its success.
A claim that "there is no conspiracy" is itself read as yet another failure to discover the plot.
Contrary evidence is read in the same way: it is reinterpreted as fabricated by the conspirators and, once discredited, leaves the claim with no evidence at all.

Missing and contrary evidence are thus rendered by the conspiracy as nondiagnostic, and any claim can be shielded from disconfirmation (or made selfsealing) by wrapping it in a conspiratorial layer that explains both why the evidence for it is missing and why evidence against it cannot be trusted (Nera et al., 2026).

text.text: We call this layer the conspiratorial wrapper.
Figure 1 illustrates the wrapper with the unsubstantiated claim that "placing a halved onion in a room prevents the flu".
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> illustrates the wrapper with the unsubstantiated claim that "placing a halved onion in a room prevents the flu".

text.text: Read as a bare claim, the absence of evidence ("no clinical evidence exists") and the existence of contrary evidence ("clinical studies show no effect beyond placebo") leave it either unsubstantiated or refuted.
Once it is wrapped in the allegation that "Big Pharma buries the evidence for remedies it cannot patent", both evidential states are neutralized: they no longer count against the claim.

Because conspiratorial allegations are not constrained by the evidence, they have potentially unbounded degrees of freedom: the wrapper can be applied to any event or aspect of reality, and, for each, it can support multiple, even mutually incompatible, hypotheses accounting for the absence of evidence for the claim it serves.

In Figure 1, both evidential states yield the same conclusion that the plot is working; whether scientists are complicit or threatened does not matter, because these logically incompatible hypotheses are rendered compatible by the overarching assumption that the truth is being concealed (Lewandowsky, Cook, & Lloyd, 2018; Nera & Schöpfer, 2023; Nera & Sutton, 2025).

text.text: Once the conspiracy extends to such a large network of actors, it can be used as a template to explain other wrongdoings.

From the concealed curative properties of onions, to Big Pharma's involvement in the development of the coronavirus, and the CIA's role in the JFK assassination, each CT can serve as evidence for other CTs, even if topically unrelated.

Indeed, conspiratorial texts accumulate topically unrelated but mutually reinforcing "evidence", linking diverse actors, events, and domains within broader explanatory frameworks (Miani et al., 2022; Tangherlini et al., 2020; Tuters & Willaert, 2022).

text.text: Yet, although topically diverse, conspiratorial discourse relies on a recogniz-able linguistic style.

Its vocabulary centers on deception, dominance, power, aggression, and death, with ingroup-outgroup framing, negative emotions, and rhetorical questions (Klein et al., 2019; Miani et al., 2021); phrases such as "the truth is hidden" and "it's a cover-up" are a staple (Recordare et al., 2024).

text.text: Any topic can generate both misinformation and CTs.

Unlike CTs, however, misinformation often presents as a bare factual claim, with no recognizable structure that separates a false claim from a true one (e.g., "the Earth is flat" vs. "the Earth is a geoid").
Linguistic markers of misinformation have been identified, but results are mixed (see e.g., Lebernegg et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Linguistic markers of misinformation have been identified, but results are mixed (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lebernegg et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More recognizable are the rhetorical techniques that often accompany misinformation (e.g., emotionally manipulative language, false dichotomies), and learning to spot them improves resilience against misinformation (Roozenbeek et al., 2022).

text.text: However they manipulate a claim, these techniques do not alter its relationship to truth.
CTs, by contrast, are embedded in a specific narrative structure that not only makes them highly recognizable but also shapes their relationship to truth.
The structure of CTs grants them a heightened resistance to disconfirmation.

Any strongly held belief resists disconfirmation (Boudry & Braeckman, 2010; Nera et al., 2026), for instance through ad hoc hypotheses introduced after the fact ("prayers did not heal because you did not believe enough").

text.text: In CTs, however, that resistance is built into the claim itself: the wrapper states in advance why evidence is missing and why contrary evidence cannot be trusted (whereas the prayer excuse is added only after the failure).
Although missing and contrary evidence can still accumulate and make a CT progressively less probable (Grimes, 2016), contrary evidence cannot refute the CT conclusively.

text.text: CTs share with unsubstantiated misinformation one trait: the absence of decisive evidence.
It is therefore tempting to treat CTs as a sub-class of misinformation.
The key difference is in how the epistemic gap can be closed.
In misinformation, evidence closes the gap because the claim can be either confirmed or disconfirmed.
In CTs, instead, the wrapper renders the absence of evidence non-diagnostic, so the gap stays open.
Note that the wrapper makes the claim resistant to disconfirmation, but not to confirmation.

Under a taxonomy based on the relationship to truth, CTs are therefore a distinct class and cannot be included in misinformation. 4 The contrast is sharpest when two claims share an identical factual core: (A) the Earth is flat (B) the Earth is flat and space agencies have faked the evidence Claim (A) is misinformation: it says how the Earth is shaped, and it can be checked against the evidence (it is false).

text.text: Claim (B) adds the wrapper, which says why that evidence is not found.
The problem we try to solve is that, on a pragmatic reading, (A) and (B) are equally false and equally conspiratorial.
Both stand so far from the available evidence that neither can be held unless one also assumes that the evidence has been corrupted.

But if we allow (A) into the class of CTs, then the same classification applies to any claim contradicted by the evidence, such as "homeopathy works", whose acceptance likewise requires assuming that available evidence cannot be trusted.
Such a pragmatic inference would thus turn every false or unsubstantiated claim into a CT, and perpetuate the very conflation documented at the start of this chapter.
We avoid this conflation by applying a semantic (vs. pragmatic) reading, thus requiring the wrapper to be present in the claim.
In doing so, we prevent bare misinformation ("homeopathy works") from being conflated with a CT ("homeopathy works, and Big Pharma buries the evidence for remedies it cannot patent").
This literal reading also spares us from inferring the beliefs a claim invites, which are external to the claim itself and of little use in a claim-based taxonomy.

Note, however, that one limitation of this approach is that restricting the analysis to what claims assert leaves misleadingness outside its reach (e.g., cherry-picking: "global temperatures fell from 2016 to 2018"), since misleadingness is by definition a contextual property.
We suggested a demarcation based on the structural properties of claims: misinformation is a bare factual claim, whereas a CT is a bare claim embedded in a conspiratorial wrapper.

We therefore define a conspiracy theory as: a claim wrapped in an explicit allegation that a conspiracy (a secretly coordinated deception against the public interest) accounts for the absence of evidence This definition is compositional: a CT is the conjunction of a bare claim and the conspiratorial wrapper.
Without the wrapper, the claim may be false or unsubstantiated, but not a CT.

Each component has its own evidential status: 𝐶 = the bare claim (e.g., "homeopathy works") and 𝑊 = the wrapper, i.e., the allegation of concealment (e.g., "Big Pharma buries the evidence for remedies it cannot patent").

𝐶 may stand in any relation to the evidence, and so may 𝑊: the wrapper can be more or less substantiated (e.g., by documented past cover-ups in the same industry), but as long as decisive evidence is missing, its role in the CT is the same.
Because 𝑊 states in advance why evidence for 𝐶 is missing and why evidence against it cannot be trusted, the CT as a whole (𝐶 + 𝑊) becomes resistant to disconfirmation, though not to confirmation.
From this compositional logic, it follows that a wrapper alone is a generic allegation of concealment with no specific claim to be shielded.
This logic parallels existing conspiracy scales adding content along a continuum of specificity.

For example, generic conspiracist scales largely consist of bare wrappers (Imhoff, 2026), which explain why information is missing without naming what is missing or who is hiding it (e.g., "the official version of the events given by the authorities very often hides the truth", Lantian et al., 2016; "many very important things happen in the world, which the public is never informed about", Bruder et al., 2013).

text.text: At the specific end of the continuum, the wrapper is attached to a bare claim about a particular event, which yields a CT in our sense (e.g., "in July 1947, the US military recovered the wreckage of an alien craft from Roswell, New Mexico, and covered up the fact", Swami et al., 2010).

text.text: In short, a bare claim may be misinformation, a bare wrapper expresses a generic conspiracist belief, and only their conjunction makes a CT.

Our definition requires the wrapper to be explicitly asserted (vs. inferred), keeping classification at the level of claims rather than beliefs and preventing the pragmatic conflation discussed above.
Some formulations imply concealment without asserting it.
In "the industry doesn't want you to know", a preference for secrecy does not entail that anyone can, or did, actually hide the truth.
Under a semantic reading, such formulations are borderline weak wrappers; where the threshold lies is, in our view, an empirical question.
In our definition, the wrapper accounts for the absence of evidence; this is what distinguishes CTs from documented accounts of conspiracies (hereafter, documented conspiracies).
Both are claims, but only in CTs does the concealment allegation explain why decisive evidence is missing.
When the concealment fails, as in documented conspiracies, and decisive evidence emerges, the allegation no longer explains any absence, and the concealment itself becomes part of what is documented.
In 1972, a claim that the White House was covering up its involvement in the Watergate break-in was a CT but once the tapes were released, the CT became a documented conspiracy.
Because the wrapper blocks disconfirmation but not confirmation, this is how a CT typically leaves the class: by being confirmed rather than refuted.
Note that among CTs, claims can also be more or less substantiated.

A laboratory origin of SARS-CoV-2 is biologically possible and has received serious scientific scrutiny, even though the available evidence favors a natural origin (Lewandowsky et al., 2023); claims about reptilian elites have no such standing.

text.text: Both, however, are CTs whenever they include a wrapper accounting for the absence of decisive evidence (e.g., that the laboratory's records were concealed).
Our demarcation predicts a sharp asymmetry in how misinformation and CTs respond to correction.
Because misinformation is truth-apt, it creates an epistemic gap that correction can, in principle, close.
By contrast, the conspiratorial wrapper keeps that gap open because it explains away disconfirming information in advance.

Moreover, the high portability of CTs predicts that debunking itself can be recruited into the conspiracy narrative, filling one of its open slots and absorbing debunkers and fact-checkers as accomplices (Poth & Dolega, 2023; Sunstein & Vermeule, 2009).

text.text: This idea, however, remains untested.
What is empirically supported, instead, is a broader asymmetry: CTs are substantially harder to correct than misinformation (though not impossible; Costello et al., 2024).

text.text: Directly negating a CT is among the least effective interventions documented in the literature (O'Mahony et al., 2023), and the meta-analytic effect size of CT correction is smaller than that of misinformation correction (Stasielowicz, 2025).

text.text: We believe this asymmetry rests on the semantic difference between bare and wrapped claims.
Piliousis and Gardikiotis (2026) paired climate-change items with explicit conspiracy content with misinformation items.
Conspiracy items were predicted by conspiracy-related constructs such as powerlessness, anthropomorphism, anomie, whereas misinformation items were predicted by political ideology alone.

Zwolinski (2024) manipulated misinformation and conspiratorial claims across matched topics and delivered a direct factual correction; after debunking, endorsement of misinformation claims dropped, while endorsement of conspiratorial claims remained unchanged.
If a conspiracy is inferred from a bare misinformation claim, as a pragmatic reading would suggest, bare and wrapped claims should behave alike, because the wrapper would be implied in both.
Yet, as these studies show, they have different predictors and respond differently to correction (Piliousis & Gardikiotis, 2026; Zwolinski, 2024).

text.text: Indeed, denying that climate change is occurring does not necessarily imply a conspiracy: one may simply give more weight to the memory of a cool summer than to scientists' warnings; yet endorsing the claim that the mainstream climate narrative is a malicious plan signals a commitment to both the claim and its wrapper.
These findings suggest that respondents do not, by default, read a conspiracy into bare claims.

Further, though indirect, support for this view comes from one of our studies (Miani, Adornetti, et al., 2026), in which participants described the events depicted in a movie ambiguous enough to leave questions unanswered and to invite a conspiratorial interpretation.

text.text: When their narratives were scored for conspiratorial content using large language models (LLMs), participants higher in conspiracy mentality did not write more conspiratorial accounts, suggesting that, absent an explicit wrapper, even those predisposed to conspiracism did not read a conspiracy into the events.

The distinction between bare and wrapped claims also appears in how LLMs themselves handle content. Bates et al. (2026) prompted six LLMs to rewrite fact-checked false claims and snippets from conspiracy articles in a journalistic style.

text.text: They found that LLMs were more likely to rewrite the conspiratorial snippets (e.g., "Concerns have been articulated regarding the…") than the fact-checked false claims, which were more often deflected or rebutted (e.g., "There is no credible evidence to support claims that…").

This pattern is tentatively consistent with the structural distinction drawn above: LLM safety mechanisms were less often engaged by conspiratorial framing, possibly because conspiratorial content explains away the absence of evidence rather than asserting a false but testable claim.
The lack of a shared taxonomy of misinformation and CTs has repercussions for both detection and psychometric tools.
Testing the wrapper as a core feature of CTs, along with other definitional features (Douglas & Sutton, 2023), is therefore a warranted empirical effort.

text.text: Researchers could cross the presence of the bare claim (𝐶; "vaccines kill"), the bare wrapper (𝑊; "evidence is suppressed"), and their conjunction (𝐶 +𝑊; "evidence that vaccines kill is suppressed").

Such a design (an improvement from the unmatched items in Piliousis and Gardikiotis, 2026) would allow researchers to test whether the wrapper changes endorsement of the same claim, and whether it improves the content and criterion validity of existing scales.
Because a CT is, by our definition, the conjunction of a claim and a wrapper, items measuring CTs are necessarily double-barreled.
This is usually considered a methodological flaw, since agreement with 𝐶 + 𝑊 does not reveal which component is endorsed.

Yet double-barreled CT items are already common in existing scales (e.g., "In July 1947, the US military recovered the wreckage of an alien craft from Roswell, New Mexico, and covered up the fact"; Swami et al., 2010), and they are unavoidable if CTs, rather than their components, are to be measured.

text.text: In a fully crossed design, the double-barreled item becomes informative: comparing it with its components separates endorsement of a CT (𝐶 + 𝑊) from endorsement of a bare claim (𝐶) and from generic conspiracist worldview (𝑊).
Paired stimuli can also extend research on motivated cognition.
When a belief is challenged, a believer can either engage with the counter-evidence or dismiss its source by recruiting a conspiratorial explanation.

In one study (Lewandowsky, 2021), endorsement of conspiratorial explanations of the scientific consensus (in our terms, wrappers) tracked dispositional conspiracism for vaccine safety but political worldview for climate change, consistent with conspiracies being recruited to sidestep an inconvenient fact.
text.formatted: In one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lewandowsky, 2021)</ref>, endorsement of conspiratorial explanations of the scientific consensus (in our terms, wrappers) tracked dispositional conspiracism for vaccine safety but political worldview for climate change, consistent with conspiracies being recruited to sidestep an inconvenient fact.

text.text: Experimentally manipulating ideological threat would test this mechanism causally and shed light on potential conspiratorial backfire effects.

For example, after debunking homeopathy, a believer's endorsement of a wrapped claim ("medical experts silence homeopathy's healing effects because homeopathy threatens their power") is expected to increase relative to its bare counterpart ("homeopathy stimulates a healing response").

This increase should occur only after corrections of personally relevant beliefs (e.g., not after "octopuses have three hearts"), reflecting the deployment of a "conspiracy for convenience" (Lewandowsky, 2021).
text.formatted: This increase should occur only after corrections of personally relevant beliefs (e.g., not after "octopuses have three hearts"), reflecting the deployment of a "conspiracy for convenience" <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lewandowsky, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The goal of this chapter was to separate CTs from misinformation, two concepts that are often used interchangeably in research and measurement.
We believe the problem of such confusion lies in the pragmatic interpretation of claims.
We therefore pitched our demarcation at the level of claims rather than beliefs, on a single criterion: a claim's relationship to truth, as determined by its structure and content.
In misinformation, a class of truth-apt claims, the epistemic gap can be closed by evidence.

In CTs, instead, the content itself explains why the evidence is missing and reduces any contrary evidence to that same absence, making the claim resistant to disconfirmation and, with it, to correction.
Research on interventions supports this distinction.

By separating the two, we provided a misinformation-aware definition of CTs, which also distinguishes CTs from documented conspiracies without stipulating that CTs are false: a claim stops being a CT once decisive evidence emerges and its wrapper no longer accounts for any absence.
This definition is empirically testable and opens new methodological possibilities.
A final note is warranted on the near-invincible explanatory power of CTs.
That CTs render contrary evidence non-diagnostic does not mean that they have the same epistemic status as more plausible explanations, including the accounts they oppose.
Resistance to disconfirmation does not mean probably true.
In fact, CTs are epistemically more demanding than their non-conspiratorial counterparts.

A conspiracy claim does not stand alone but drags with it a system of auxiliary hypotheses (Lewandowsky, Lloyd, & Brophy, 2018; Wagner-Egger et al., 2019), each of which must hold for the theory to survive.

text.text: The number of people needed to be kept silent makes large-scale conspiracies intrinsically prone to failure (Grimes, 2016), further lowering their prior probability.
